sections.title: What is String Matching?
sections.content:
String matching finds all occurrences of pattern P in text T. Brute force is O(|T| × |P|). Three classical algorithms do better.

**KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt)** achieves O(|T| + |P|) by precomputing a **failure function** that encodes how much of the pattern can be reused after a mismatch. When mismatch occurs at position j in P, instead of restarting from 0, KMP jumps j back to `fail[j-1]`. The text pointer never moves backward.

**Z-algorithm** also O(|T| + |P|). Computes Z[i] = length of longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. To find P in T: concatenate P+'$'+T, compute Z-array, positions where Z[i] >= |P| are matches. Arguably simpler to implement than KMP.

**Rabin-Karp** uses polynomial **rolling hash** to compare substrings in O(1) by sliding a window. Expected O(|T| + |P|). Main advantage: easy extension to multiple pattern search and longest common substring.

In most interviews, KMP is sufficient. Z-algorithm and Rabin-Karp appear more in competitive programming.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use string matching algorithms when brute-force O(|T|×|P|) is too slow — typically when |T| or |P| exceeds 10^4. KMP is the standard interview algorithm. Z-algorithm for 'shortest repeating unit' and palindrome problems. Rabin-Karp for multiple pattern search.

sections.title: KMP Failure Function, Z-Algorithm, and Rabin-Karp
sections.content:
## KMP Failure Function

`fail[i]` = length of the longest **proper** prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix. `fail[0] = 0` always.

Building in O(|P|):
```
fail[0]=0; j=0;
for i from 1 to |P|-1:
  while j>0 && P[i]!==P[j]: j=fail[j-1]  // fall back
  if P[i]===P[j]: j++
  fail[i]=j
```
On mismatch at j, jump to `fail[j-1]` not `j--`.

## KMP Search

Two pointers i (T, never moves back) and j (P):
- Match: advance both.
- Mismatch + j>0: `j=fail[j-1]`, don't advance i.
- Mismatch + j===0: advance i only.
- j===|P|: match found. `j=fail[j-1]` to continue for overlapping matches.

## Z-Algorithm

`Z[i]` = length of longest substring at S[i] matching a prefix of S. Maintain window [L,R] (rightmost Z-box):
- If i < R: `Z[i]=min(R-i, Z[i-L])` as starting point.
- Extend Z[i] by direct comparison.
- Update [L,R] if i+Z[i]-1 > R.

Pattern matching: S = P+'$'+T. Z[i] >= |P| in T portion → match.

## Rabin-Karp

Polynomial hash. Sliding window update (drop leftmost char, add rightmost):
`newHash = (oldHash - S[0]*base^(L-1)) * base + newChar`
O(1) per slide. Verify with string comparison on hash match to handle collisions.

## Shortest Repeating Unit

If `|P| % (|P| - fail[|P|-1]) === 0`, the shortest repeating unit has length `|P| - fail[|P|-1]`.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Full KMP (failure function + search) and Z-algorithm (Z-array + search). Both return all match indices in O(|T|+|P|). The '$' separator in zSearch prevents the Z-box from spanning the pattern-text boundary.

items.name: Shortest Palindrome via KMP
items.description: Concatenate S+'#'+reverse(S) and compute the KMP failure function. The last value of fail gives the longest prefix of S that is a palindrome — characters outside must be prepended in reverse.

items.name: Repeated Substring Pattern
items.description: A string S has a repeating unit if S.length % (S.length - fail[S.length-1]) === 0. Build the failure function on S itself — no separate text needed.

items.name: Longest Happy Prefix via KMP
items.description: Longest happy prefix = longest string that is both prefix and suffix of S (excluding S). This is exactly fail[|S|-1] from the KMP failure function.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(|T|+|P|) KMP and Z-algorithm; O(|T|+|P|) expected Rabin-Karp
sections.space: O(|P|) for KMP failure function; O(|T|+|P|) for Z on concatenated string
sections.explanation: KMP failure function: j only increments |P| times total and can only decrease, bounding total iterations to O(|P|). Search is O(|T|) by same argument. Z-algorithm: each character processed at most twice — once when Z-box extends past it, once when inside a Z-box used as lookup. Rabin-Karp: O(|P|) preprocessing, O(|T|) sliding window, but hash collisions cause O(|P|) verification — expected O(|T|+|P|), worst case O(|T|×|P|).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: KMP failure function: fail[0]=0 always. Start build loop at i=1, not i=0.
On mismatch during failure function build: use j=fail[j-1] not j--. Using j-- makes the build O(|P|^2) and computes wrong values.
KMP finds overlapping matches by default via j=fail[j-1] after a match. Resetting j=0 after a match gives non-overlapping count — correct for that use case, wrong for all-occurrences.
Rabin-Karp without collision verification: different strings can hash identically. Always verify hash matches with direct string comparison. Without it, false positives are reported.
Z-array Z[0] is the full string length by convention. Do not use Z[0] as a match indicator in the search phase — all positions i >= pattern.length+1 should be checked against |pattern|.

items.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
items.why: Direct KMP application — implement full KMP search and return the first match index.

items.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
items.why: Failure function period detection — derive repeating unit length from |S|-fail[|S|-1] and check divisibility.

items.title: Shortest Palindrome
items.why: KMP on concatenated string — non-obvious application of fail on S+'#'+reverse(S) to find the longest palindromic prefix.

items.title: Longest Happy Prefix
items.why: Direct failure function query — the answer is fail[|S|-1], testing deep understanding of what fail[i] encodes.
